design_detail: NeuroView opinion essay in Neuron (4 pages, 7 references, 4 of them by the author) written after the police killing of George Floyd. It argues that researchers exaggerate the harmful effects of recreational drugs on the brain, that such exaggeration has been used to justify police violence against Black people, and it proposes five practical steps for scientists and institutions. No methods or data; its drug-science statements are cited to the author's 2013 trade book (High Price), to a 2012 critical review he led, to one human laboratory study of intranasal methamphetamine and to an article he co-wrote.
can_establish: What the author argues, and that he holds that 70% to 90% of people who use heroin or methamphetamine do not meet criteria for a substance use disorder and that no neurobiological substrate of addiction has been identified.
cannot_establish: The 70% to 90% figure itself (sourced only to his own book), whether brain differences between people who use drugs and people who do not exist or matter, or any causal link between neuroscientific claims and police killings: none is shown with data in the piece.

sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria. Seven references: the author's book (Hart, 2013), a human laboratory study of intranasal methamphetamine (Hart et al., 2008), a critical review of cognitive functioning in people who use methamphetamine (Hart et al., 2012), an article on the opioid crisis and racism (Hart & Hart, 2019), a news site's figures on the Philippine drug war (Bueza, 2017), 2020 statements by the Society for Neuroscience and by the NIDA director, and the review by Volkow, Koob and McLellan (2016) (p. 218, References).
sample.selection_effects: Four of the seven references are the author's; every statement about drug effects, addiction and the brain rests on them. The opposing view is represented by one sentence quoted from Volkow et al. (2016) (p. 217).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. Drugs named: heroin, methamphetamine, crack cocaine, cannabis (marijuana) and ketamine.

comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not addressed. The author attributes brain differences between people who use drugs and people who do not to normal human variability (p. 218), without discussing whether such differences predate drug use.

outcomes.operationalization: Addiction: drug use that causes some people significant distress and problems that impair their ability to function, which the author calls the most common definition and equates with DSM-5 substance use disorder (p. 216). Brain damage: not defined; he uses it for researchers' reading of group brain differences as deficits representing substantial loss of function (p. 218).

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The only drug-use figure: most people, 70% to 90%, who use even the most stigmatized drugs, such as heroin and methamphetamine, do not meet criteria for a substance use disorder (p. 216), cited to the author's book (Hart, 2013); no survey, population, year, time frame or diagnostic definition is given.
analysis.selective_reporting: Evidence for neurobiological models of addiction is represented by a single quoted sentence (Volkow et al., 2016; p. 217) and dismissed; no study supporting those models is described. The statement that drug effects are overwhelmingly positive rests on one laboratory study of one drug (p. 217).

interpretation_gap.results_show: No results. The empirical statements are cited to the author's own book (70% to 90% do not meet criteria for a use disorder; Black people are more likely to be arrested), a review he led (no identified neurobiological substrate of addiction; brain differences within normal variability), one laboratory study of intranasal methamphetamine (drug effects overwhelmingly positive) and an article he co-wrote (similar rates of drug use and selling by race).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title and abstract say that exaggerating harmful drug effects on the brain is killing Black people and has led to disproportionately high Black incarceration and countless deaths (p. 215). The text says there is no solid evidence that human recreational drug use causes brain damage, no credible evidence that addiction is caused by a brain abnormality, and absolutely no scientific evidence in humans for the claim of Volkow et al. (2016) that early drug use can erode control (p. 217); none of these sentences cites a study except Hart et al. (2012), a review about cognition in people who use methamphetamine. 'Recreational drug effects are overwhelmingly positive' generalizes from one methamphetamine study to recreational drugs as a class (p. 217). On p. 218 the categorical statement that brain differences between groups reflect the normal range of human variability is followed by the weaker restatement that brain differences do not necessarily mean brain damage. The causal chain from neuroscientific claims to police killings is argued through cases, a criminal complaint and statements by officials, not tested.

timeline.event: Human laboratory study of intranasal methamphetamine (Hart et al., 2008), the only study the essay cites for recreational drug effects being overwhelmingly positive (not read for this card).

Critical review of cognitive functioning in people who use methamphetamine (Hart et al., 2012), cited by the essay for the absence of an identified neurobiological substrate of addiction, for brain-imaging pictures without data, and for group brain differences reflecting normal variability (not read for this card).

Review of US national surveys: most people who had ever met criteria for drug dependence did not meet them in the past year; it also notes that DSM criteria separate groups by neural activity (Heyman, 2013, p. 34), a group-level difference the essay does not address directly.
Volkow, Koob and McLellan, New England Journal of Medicine review of neurobiological advances from the brain disease model of addiction, quoted as the claim Hart disputes (no project record).
Hart's earlier opinion column making the same argument; here described as an open letter to NIDA that fell on deaf ears (p. 217).

replication.where_it_stands: An argument by a prominent researcher of drug effects, not evidence. The 70% to 90% figure needs primary population data on transition from use to a use disorder, drug by drug (project records exist for Anthony et al., 1994, and Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). The 'no neurobiological substrate' statement is sourced to a review about cognition in people who use methamphetamine (Hart et al., 2012), which must be read before the sentence is used.

funding.declared_conflicts: No declaration of interests is printed. In the text the author says NIDA has been his primary funder, that he received multimillion-dollar grants and served on prestigious neuropsychopharmacology committees, and that he benefited personally because his work aligned with NIDA's dominant perspective on drug harms (p. 216, 'Remaining Silent Is Not an Option', 3rd paragraph).
funding.affiliations_note: Carl L. Hart, Departments of Psychology and Psychiatry, Columbia University, and New York State Psychiatric Institute, Division on Substance Use (p. 215). He says his research since 1999 has involved giving thousands of doses of drugs, including crack cocaine, marijuana, ketamine and methamphetamine, to people in the laboratory (p. 216). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the argument.

what_would_settle_it: For the 70% to 90% figure: nationally representative surveys reporting, for each drug, the share of people who ever used it who ever met criteria for a use disorder, with definitions and time frames stated. For the claims about brain differences: prospective imaging before and after the start of regular use, with comparison participants scanned at the same intervals, testing whether differences predate use and whether they relate to everyday function.

domains.note: No search or criteria; seven references chosen by the author.
Cited studies are not appraised; one laboratory study of one drug is generalized to recreational drugs as a class.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Four of seven references are the author's (a trade book, a review, a laboratory study and a co-written article), and every drug-science statement rests on them.

Some statements are labelled as belief or suspicion (toxicology levels 'I believe'; researchers' motives 'I suspect'), but contested empirical statements are presented as facts ('It's just a fact'; 'absolutely no scientific evidence') without evidence shown (pp. 216–217).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on drug effects on the brain and on addiction
domains.note: Only the case that harms are exaggerated is made; evidence for neurobiological models and for lasting harm is not described.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to an opinion essay (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. An advocacy piece whose drug-science statements rest on the author's own book, review and one laboratory study. Cite it for what Hart argues and as a pointer to Hart et al. (2012), never for the 70% to 90% figure or for statements about brain damage, which need primary sources.

key_findings.finding: The author states that most people, 70% to 90%, who use even the most stigmatized drugs, such as heroin and methamphetamine, do not meet criteria for a substance use disorder, citing his own 2013 book (High Price); no survey, population, year, time frame or definition is given.
key_findings.locator: Using 'Science' to Legitimize a Massacre, 1st paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: He defines addiction as drug use that causes some people significant distress and problems that impair their ability to function, calls this the most common definition, and equates it with DSM-5 substance use disorder; he accepts that drug use can cause such problems in some people.
key_findings.locator: Using 'Science' to Legitimize a Massacre, 1st paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: From the 70% to 90% figure he draws two points: addiction represents a minority of drug effects but receives almost all the attention; and if most people who use a drug do not become addicted, the drug cannot be blamed for causing addiction, as food is not blamed for food addiction.
key_findings.locator: Using 'Science' to Legitimize a Massacre, 1st paragraph (p. 216, right column, continuing on p. 217, left column)

key_findings.finding: He states that no neurobiological substrate differentiating people with addiction from people without it has been identified (citing Hart et al., 2012), and, without a citation, that there is no solid evidence that human recreational drug use causes brain damage nor credible evidence that addiction is caused by a brain abnormality.
key_findings.locator: Using 'Science' to Legitimize a Massacre, 2nd paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: He quotes Volkow, Koob and McLellan (2016), that undetected and unchecked early voluntary drug use can lead to brain changes that erode a person's control over the impulse to take drugs, and states that there is absolutely no scientific evidence in humans to justify it; he adds that brain-imaging pictures without data are not evidence (citing Hart et al., 2012).
key_findings.locator: Using 'Science' to Legitimize a Massacre, 2nd paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: He asks why, if recreational drug use is neurotoxic, researchers including himself are allowed to give these drugs to people regularly, and states that recreational drug effects are overwhelmingly positive, citing one laboratory study of intranasal methamphetamine (Hart et al., 2008); he suspects some researchers overemphasize harms to strengthen grant applications.
key_findings.locator: Using 'Science' to Legitimize a Massacre, 3rd paragraph (left column, continuing in the middle column)

key_findings.finding: He states that neuroimaging researchers tend to read any brain differences between people who use drugs and people who do not as deficits representing substantial loss of function, whereas such differences reflect the normal range of human brain variability (citing Hart et al., 2012); restated as: brain differences do not necessarily equate to brain damage.
key_findings.locator: Practical Steps: Inaction Is Betrayal, 3rd paragraph ('Fourth', left column, continuing in the middle column)

key_findings.finding: He writes that he once wholeheartedly believed crack cocaine and heroin had destroyed certain Black communities and began studying neuroscience to solve the 'drug problem'; since 1999 his research has involved giving thousands of doses of drugs, including crack cocaine, marijuana, ketamine and methamphetamine, to people in the laboratory.
key_findings.locator: Remaining Silent Is Not an Option, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (middle and right columns)

key_findings.finding: He states that Black people suspected of drug offences are much more likely than white people to be arrested (citing his book, Hart, 2013) although both groups use and sell drugs at similar rates (citing Hart & Hart, 2019).
key_findings.locator: Using Drugs to Legitimize a Massacre, 8th paragraph (middle column)

key_findings.finding: Of the people killed by police whom he lists, he says their toxicology findings, with their behaviour, showed drug levels that he believes were too low to have contributed to their deaths; no values are given.
key_findings.locator: Using Drugs to Legitimize a Massacre, 4th paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: He proposes five steps (first to fourth, then 'finally'): watch the video of George Floyd's killing in full; stop equating talk about racism with action; institutions and journals to act against structural racism (including calls for papers on police killings of Black people); NIDA to run public campaigns against overinterpretation of neuroimaging data and against extrajudicial killings, and to present a realistic view of drug use based on human laboratory studies rather than anecdote; and researchers to avoid an unjustified, exclusive focus on negative drug effects in papers and grant applications and to advocate moving part of police budgets to health care, education and employment.
key_findings.locator: Practical Steps: Inaction Is Betrayal, 1st to 4th paragraphs (p. 217, right column, to p. 218, right column)

reporting_issues.issue: The 70% to 90% figure is cited to the author's trade book, not to a dataset, and no survey, drug-by-drug breakdown, time frame (lifetime or past year) or definition (DSM-IV dependence or abuse, or DSM-5 disorder) is given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure cannot be checked from the essay; a claim that uses it must cite primary population surveys and say which definition they used.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that no neurobiological substrate distinguishes people with and without addiction is cited to Hart et al. (2012), whose title (p. 218, References) concerns cognitive functioning in people who use methamphetamine, not biological markers of addiction across drugs.
reporting_issues.consequence: The citation may not support a general statement about addiction; Hart et al. (2012) must be read before the sentence is used.

reporting_issues.issue: 'Recreational drug effects are overwhelmingly positive' is supported by a single laboratory study of one drug given by one route (intranasal methamphetamine; Hart et al., 2008).
reporting_issues.consequence: The generalization to recreational drugs as a class goes beyond the cited evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: On p. 218 a categorical statement (brain differences between groups reflect the normal range of variability) is followed by a weaker one (brain differences do not necessarily equate to brain damage), both cited to the same review.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only the weaker statement is the kind a review could support; the categorical one is not shown.

reporting_issues.issue: The essay gives the title of the author's 2017 column as 'Viewing addiction as a brain disease promotes social injustices' and the journal as 'Nature Human Behavior' (p. 217); the column's printed title ends 'social injustice' and the journal is Nature Human Behaviour (hart_2017, p. 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite the 2017 column by its DOI.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Neuron 107, pp. 215–218 (all pages, including the reference list; read on the rendered pages; no supplement; no declaration of interests printed). Paragraphs are counted within each section heading; the opening paragraph before the first heading is not counted in any section.
